title: One came back (Luke 17:11–19)
hook: ten lepers healed, and one, a Samaritan, returns to say thank you

segments.voice: Yesterday, a rich man stepped around Lazarus every day. Your line was he was at the gate. Whose name did you learn? Day four hundred seventy-three.

A birthday is over, and a parent stands over a child with a pen and a stack of cards. Write your thank-you notes. To the child, it's a chore. A thank-you that arrives days later, unasked, saying what you did for me mattered, is a different thing. Jesus is still on the road to Jerusalem, passing between Samaria and Galilee. At the edge of a village, ten men stand far off, because their disease means they have to keep their distance. Today, the ones who didn't come back, and the one who did.
screen: `WRITE YOUR THANK-YOU NOTES.` → `SOMEONE CAME BACK TO SAY IT.` → `TEN MEN STANDING FAR OFF.`

segments.voice: They lift up their voices: Jesus, master, have mercy on us. In the Law of Moses, leprosy names a range of skin conditions, and Leviticus says the person must dwell alone, outside the camp, and cry out that he is unclean. Jesus doesn't touch them this time. He just says: go, show yourselves to the priests. That's what the Law of Moses required when someone was healed, so the priest could declare them clean and they could go home. And as they went, they were cleansed. They set off not yet healed, and somewhere on the road, they're clean. Nine keep walking. They're doing exactly what Jesus told them. "And one of them, when he saw that he was made clean, went back, with a loud voice glorifying God." He falls on his face at Jesus' feet, giving thanks. And Luke adds four words: and this was a Samaritan. The outsider. Then Jesus asks, almost to himself: "Were not ten made clean? and where are the nine?" He calls the man a stranger, a foreigner, the only one who came back to give glory to God. Then: arise, go thy way, thy faith hath made thee whole. Here's what a Catholic ear catches. Luke's Greek word for giving thanks is eucharistein, the word behind Eucharist, the name Catholics give the Mass itself. Some Catholic readers see the Samaritan, face down on the road, as a small picture of that: a healed man who turns around and gives thanks. The nine weren't bad. They were obedient. They were also in a hurry to get back to their lives. Only one stopped long enough to turn around.
screen: `TEN MEN STANDING FAR OFF.` · `HEALED WHILE WALKING.` · `ONE TURNS BACK: A SAMARITAN.` · `EUCHARISTEIN: TO GIVE THANKS.` · then, large: `WHERE ARE THE NINE?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank someone specifically. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last month. Who helped you, and you kept walking? A doctor, a teacher, a friend who listened, a stranger who held a door at the right moment. Choose one. Now get specific: what exactly did they do, and what difference did it make? Plan how you'll tell them today, by message, call or in person, in words that name the thing. If you pray, give thanks to God for them too. The bell holds the time.
Samaritan. Of ten lepers healed on the road, the one who turned around to give thanks was this outsider. Today's word.
Your line: where are the nine. Today, be the one who comes back: thank someone for one specific thing. Day four hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Catholics call the Mass the Eucharist, from the Greek for thanksgiving, and some make a short prayer of thanksgiving in silence after receiving Communion before leaving the church.

original.note: Greek: giving thanks. The root of the word Eucharist.

trapdoor: what you thought: the nine were ungrateful people who disobeyed.
what it means: the nine obeyed and were healed. only the Samaritan stopped, turned back, and gave thanks and glory to God.
what a scholar hears: Luke uses eucharisteo, the verb behind Eucharist, and calls the man allogenes, a foreigner, a word found on the Temple's warning inscription.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer tells the listener what they felt and remember; 'border between Samaria and Galilee' now follows the Douay's 'between'; leprosy line now rests on Leviticus 13:45–46; cut the invented 'halfway there' (voice and fork); 'makes the first eucharist' (garbled, a doctrinal-sounding claim) reframed as some readers' devotional reading; Eucharist etymology now cited to CCC 1328.
Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 17:15 and 17:17.
Trapdoor: allogenes appears only here in the New Testament and on the Temple balustrade inscription warning foreigners; confirm.
Leprosy as a range of skin diseases (Hebrew tsara'at) is standard; confirm.
Calling the Samaritan's thanks 'the first eucharist in this story' is a devotional observation, not a doctrinal claim; confirm acceptable.
